column2: On the authority of Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Do not envy one another, do not inflate prices against one another, do not hate one another, do not turn your backs on one another, and do not undercut one another in selling. Be, O servants of Allah, brothers. The Muslim is the brother of the Muslim:

he does not wrong him, forsake him, lie to him or hold him in contempt. Taqwā is here”—and he pointed to his chest three times. “It is evil enough for a person to hold his Muslim brother in contempt. All of the Muslim is inviolable to the Muslim: his blood, his wealth and his honour.” Reported by Muslim.

His words, “Do not envy one another, do not inflate prices against one another, do not hate one another, do not turn your backs on one another, and do not undercut one another in selling”: envy (ḥasad) occurs in matters of this world and the Hereafter.
It includes the envier's disliking a blessing Allah has bestowed on someone else, and it includes wishing that this blessing be removed from him, whether he wishes it to pass to himself or not.

But if he wishes for the like of what Allah has bestowed on another, without disliking that the other has it and without wishing it to be removed from him, that is ghibṭah (benign envy), which is not blameworthy. Najsh is bidding up the price of an item when it is being auctioned

while not wanting to buy it, but wanting to benefit the seller by raising the price for him or to harm the buyer by raising the price against him. Tabāghuḍ (mutual hatred) is engaging in the causes of hatred and doing what brings it about. Tadābur is cutting one another off and shunning one another,

so that one does not like to meet one's brother; rather, each turns his back on the other because of the hatred between them. Selling over another's sale is when two people have agreed a sale of an item and are within the option period,
and another comes to the buyer and says to him: Leave this item, and I will sell you a similar one, or a better one, for less than you bought it for. This causes mutual hatred.

His words, “Be, O servants of Allah, brothers. The Muslim is the brother of the Muslim: he does not wrong him, forsake him, lie to him or hold him in contempt. Taqwā is here—and he pointed to his chest three times.
It is evil enough for a person to hold his Muslim brother in contempt”: having forbidden unlawful things that involve hatred among the Muslims and engaging in its causes,
he ﷺ directed the Muslims to what is required of them, namely that they be brothers who love one another and are united, being gentle with one another

and kind to one another, bringing benefit to one another and warding off harm. He stressed this with his words, “The Muslim is the brother of the Muslim”, meaning that brotherhood requires that he love for others what he loves for himself

and dislike for them what he dislikes for himself. So he does not wrong another by transgressing against him or causing him any harm; he does not forsake him when he needs his support and he is able to give it;

he does not tell him something in which he is lying; and he does not hold him in contempt by belittling him and looking down on him. Then he ﷺ made clear the ugliness of a Muslim's holding his brother in contempt, saying:
“It is evil enough for a person to hold his Muslim brother in contempt”, that is, contempt for his brother is evil enough for him even if he had no other evil.
Between forbidding contempt and making clear how great its evil is, he ﷺ placed his words, “Taqwā is here”, pointing to his chest three times, that is, to the heart,

to make clear that what counts is the faith and taqwā that subsist in the hearts, and that the heart of the one held in contempt may be filled with taqwā, while the heart of the one who holds him in contempt and is arrogant towards him is otherwise.

As for those who commit open sins and, when alerted to one of them, point to their chest and say, “Taqwā is here”, it should be said to them: When taqwā is in the heart, its effect appears on the limbs in uprightness and leaving sin;
and he ﷺ said: “Indeed, in the body there is a lump of flesh which, if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Indeed, it is the heart”; and he ﷺ said:

“Allah does not look at your forms or your wealth, but He looks at your hearts and your deeds.” Reported by Muslim (2564). One of the Salaf is reported to have said: “Faith is not a matter of wishful thinking or outward show; it is what settles in the hearts and is confirmed by deeds.”

His words, “All of the Muslim is inviolable to the Muslim: his blood, his wealth and his honour”: it is unlawful to transgress against life by killing or anything less; against wealth by theft, usurpation and the like; and against honour by insulting, reviling, backbiting, talebearing and the like.
The Prophet ﷺ emphasised the inviolability of these three in the Farewell Pilgrimage, comparing their sanctity to the sanctity of time and place,
when he ﷺ said: “Your blood, your wealth and your honour are inviolable to you, like the sanctity of this day of yours, in this month of yours, in this land of yours.”
Envying one another, inflating prices, selling over one's brother's sale and likewise buying over his purchase are unlawful, as is everything that brings enmity and hatred among the Muslims.
Engaging in the causes of hatred is forbidden, as is everything that results from it, such as Muslims cutting one another off and shunning one another.
All Muslims are urged to be brothers who love one another and are united.
Brotherhood among the Muslims requires bringing good to them and warding off harm from them.
It is unlawful for a Muslim to wrong his brother, forsake him, hold him in contempt or lie to him.
A Muslim's holding his brother in contempt is dangerous: it is evil enough for the one who does it, even if he has no other evil.
The measure of superiority among people is taqwā, as Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: “Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you” [al-Ḥujurāt 49:13].
The place of taqwā is the heart, as in this hadith and in the words of the Exalted: “That [is so]. And whoever honours the symbols of Allah—indeed, it is from the taqwā of hearts” [al-Ḥajj 22:32].
The effects of taqwā in the hearts appear on the limbs, and by the soundness of the hearts the rest of the body is sound.
Transgressing against the Muslims in their blood, wealth and honour is unlawful.
